messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 26
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Fisherman
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 37

# The Weight of the Water

Marcus is twenty-six years old, broad-shouldered and weathered in the way that men who work the sea tend to be, though his weathering runs deeper than sun and salt. He has been married to his wife, Lena, for two years. He fishes the North Sea out of a small port town in the Netherlands, working long shifts aboard a commercial trawler, and on most mornings he is on the water before the rest of the town has stirred. It is, he says, the only place he still feels something close to himself.

Three years ago, Marcus was traveling through a region of Eastern Europe during what was supposed to be a brief overland trip between countries. He was detained at a remote checkpoint by a paramilitary group, held for eleven days, and subjected to repeated physical and psychological torture — beatings, stress positions, sleep deprivation, and threats of execution. He was eventually released without explanation, left at the edge of a road with no identification and no clear understanding of why any of it had happened. He made his way home. He told almost no one the full story. He married Lena six months later, believing, or perhaps hoping, that forward motion was the same thing as healing.

It was not.

The first winter back on the boat, Marcus noticed that the sound of the winch — a low, grinding mechanical groan — would sometimes stop him completely. His hands would still be moving, coiling rope or sorting catch, but he would be somewhere else entirely: back in a concrete room, wrists bound, waiting. These episodes last only seconds, but they leave him shaken and disoriented in a way he finds humiliating among his crewmates. He has become skilled at disguising them, stepping to the rail and staring at the water until the present reasserts itself.

At home, the nights are harder. Marcus sleeps lightly and poorly, waking often at sounds that mean nothing — a car door, a neighbor's dog — with his heart hammering and his body already halfway out of bed. He has had the same dream dozens of times: he is in the room again, but in the dream he cannot remember how long he has been there or whether anyone knows where he is. He wakes from it with the specific, terrible certainty that he has been forgotten. Lena has learned not to touch him in those first moments of waking. Early on, she did, and he reacted badly. He is still ashamed of that.

He describes himself as irritable in a way that feels foreign to him. He grew up in a family that was, by his account, calm and close, and he does not recognize the man who snaps at Lena over small things, who finds the noise of a crowded bar intolerable, who sometimes sits in his truck in the driveway for ten minutes before he can bring himself to go inside. He avoids news coverage of conflict or detention. He avoids a particular stretch of highway that passes a concrete overpass whose shadow, on certain afternoons, falls across the road at an angle that reminds him of something he cannot fully name.

What Marcus finds most difficult to articulate — and what seems to trouble him most — is a persistent sense of flatness. He loves Lena, he says this plainly, but there are days when that love feels like something he knows intellectually rather than feels. He used to enjoy things: football, cooking, the particular satisfaction of a good haul. Those pleasures have not disappeared entirely, but they arrive muted, as if from a distance.

He comes to sessions on his days off the water, still smelling faintly of brine. He is thoughtful, careful with his words, and quietly determined to understand what has happened to him. The sea, he says, does not care what happened to him, and that is exactly why he keeps going back.
